expectedText:
TRANSFER OF A DECEDENT'S FIREARM BY OPERATION OF LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan Rivera · March 4, 2026

FIREARMS IN A CALIFORNIA ESTATE: THE OPERATION-OF-LAW EXEMPTION
This information sheet describes California law governing how a firearm owned by Pat Morgan Rivera, who died on March 4, 2026, may pass to Jordan Rivera as personal representative, to Casey Rivera as trustee, to Alex Rivera as surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, or to another person whose relationship to Pat Morgan Rivera is Adult child, without that transfer being completed through a licensed firearms dealer. It concerns Smith & Wesson Model 10 revolver, .38 Special, serial number ABC1234 only to the extent that description is relevant to identifying the firearm in any report the exemption discussed here requires. This sheet states facts about a specific statutory exemption and the conditions attached to it; it does not determine whether any specific person is in fact eligible to receive a specific firearm under that exemption.

BASELINE RULE: PRIVATE FIREARM TRANSFERS GO THROUGH A LICENSED DEALER
California law states a general rule for firearm transactions between two people who are neither one a licensed dealer: the transaction must be completed through a licensed firearms dealer. This baseline rule is the rule that a separate statutory exemption, addressed in this information sheet's other clauses, departs from for a defined set of estate-related transfers, including certain transfers to Jordan Rivera, Casey Rivera, and Alex Rivera.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Where neither party to the transaction holds a dealer’s license issued pursuant to Sections 26700 to 26915, inclusive, the parties to the transaction shall complete the sale, loan, or transfer of that firearm through a licensed firearms dealer pursuant to Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 28050)."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 27545 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=27545)
  Known gap: Penal Code § 27545 is quoted here as California's single statutory statement of the general dealer-transfer requirement; the section itself states only that requirement, and does not list any exemption -- the operation-of-law exemption this document otherwise addresses appears in a separate statutory section, quoted in this document's other clauses, not in § 27545 itself. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own baseline private-party transfer rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not a claim that every state routes private firearm transfers through a dealer.

WHICH ESTATE-RELATED TRANSFERS COUNT AS “BY OPERATION OF LAW”
California's Penal Code defines the phrase “a person taking title or possession of a firearm by operation of law” through a list of specific, separately lettered instances. Several of those instances arise directly out of administering a decedent's estate or trust: an estate's executor, personal representative, or administrator, where the estate includes a firearm; a firearm passing to a surviving spouse under the Probate Code's provisions for property passing to a surviving spouse; the trustee of a trust that includes a firearm and that was created within a will; and a firearm passed to a decedent's successor under the Probate Code's provisions for succession to a decedent's property. Each is a separately defined statutory instance, not a general catch-all covering any transfer connected to a death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the phrase “a person taking title or possession of a firearm by operation of law” includes, but is not limited to, any of the following instances in which an individual receives title to, or possession of, a firearm:(a) The executor, personal representative, or administrator of an estate, if the estate includes a firearm."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 16990(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=16990)
  "(h) A firearm passing to a surviving spouse pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 13500) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Probate Code."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 16990(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=16990)
  "(k) The trustee of a trust that includes a firearm and that was part of a will that created the trust.(l) A firearm passed to a decedent’s successor pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 13000) of Division 8 of the Probate Code."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 16990(k)-(l) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=16990)
  Known gap: § 16990 defines the phrase through 19 separately lettered instances in total; this clause quotes only the four connected to administering a decedent's estate or trust -- subdivisions (a), (h), (k), and (l). It does not restate the other 15 lettered instances the same section defines, which cover secured creditors, levying officers, receivers, bankruptcy trustees, assignees for the benefit of creditors, a Family Code § 850 transmutation of property between spouses, two separate law-enforcement-related transfers, a person acting under a power of attorney, a conservator, a guardian ad litem, a court-supervised trust, a trust not falling under subdivisions (k) or (p), a special administrator, and a guardian -- none of which is a routine decedent estate or trust administration category in the way subdivisions (a), (h), (k), and (l) are. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California itself defines this phrase -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, and not a claim that a firearm passing to any of these persons is automatically transferred free of every other condition; the separate conditions the exemption itself imposes are addressed in this information sheet's other clauses. Formatting correction made during integration review: the delivered quotes for subdivision (a) and for subdivisions (k)-(l) originally inserted a space at the transition between the introductory colon/period and the following subdivision letter (e.g., "firearm: (a)"); the actual leginfo.legislature.ca.gov source has no character at all between the punctuation and the opening parenthesis (only a non-breaking space after each letter, already normalized elsewhere in this document), confirmed identical across two independently fetched copies of the section. The inserted space has been removed so the quote matches the source exactly.

THE EXEMPTION'S OWN CONDITIONS, INCLUDING A 30-DAY DOJ REPORT
A separate statutory section exempts a person taking title or possession of a firearm by operation of law from the general dealer-transfer requirement, but only where that person is not prohibited by state or federal law from possessing, receiving, owning, or purchasing a firearm, and only where the section's own additional conditions are met. For most people receiving a firearm this way -- including Jordan Rivera as personal representative and Casey Rivera as trustee -- one of those conditions is a report to the Department of Justice, to be submitted within 30 days of taking possession, that includes information about the individual taking possession, how title or possession was obtained and from whom, and a description of the firearm in question.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "(a) Section 27545 does not apply to a person who takes title or possession of a firearm by operation of law if the person is not prohibited by state or federal law from possessing, receiving, owning, or purchasing a firearm and all of the following conditions are met:"
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 27920(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=27920)
  "the person shall, within 30 days of taking possession, submit a report to the Department of Justice, in a manner prescribed by the department, that includes information concerning the individual taking possession of the firearm, how title or possession was obtained and from whom, and a description of the firearm in question."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 27920(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=27920)
  Known gap: This clause addresses the general reporting condition in § 27920(a)(1); it does not restate the section's separate condition for a person receiving a firearm under subdivision (g), (h), (l), or (q) of § 16990, who instead faces the two-part condition in § 27920(a)(2) (a DOJ report plus a firearm safety certificate obtained before taking possession), nor the distinct Automated Firearms System entry conditions in § 27920(a)(3) and (a)(4) that apply to certain law-enforcement-related transfers, which this document does not otherwise address. It also does not determine whether a personal representative, trustee, surviving spouse, or any other specific person is in fact a person 'not prohibited by state or federal law' from possessing a firearm -- that determination turns on facts about the specific person, separate from the estate-administration facts this document addresses, and a separate statute (Penal Code § 29800 and its neighboring sections, among others) independently defines who is a prohibited person, which this document does not restate.

BRINGING AN OUT-OF-STATE DECEDENT'S FIREARM INTO CALIFORNIA
A related but separate statutory provision addresses a different scenario: a firearm located outside California when Pat Morgan Rivera died, later brought into the state. One part of that provision exempts an executor, personal representative, or administrator, or the trustee of a will-created trust, who acquires ownership of a firearm in that capacity, from California's general restriction on importing a firearm into the state, subject to the provision's own conditions. A separate part of the same provision states a parallel exemption for a surviving spouse or surviving registered domestic partner who acquires ownership of the firearm by bequest or intestate succession.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "(1) The person acquires ownership of the firearm as an executor, personal representative, or administrator of an estate, or as the trustee of a trust that includes a firearm and that was part of a will that created the trust."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 27920(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=27920)
  "(1) The person acquires ownership of the firearm by bequest or intestate succession as a surviving spouse or as the surviving registered domestic partner of the decedent who owned that firearm."
  — California Penal Code (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Penal Code § 27920(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=27920)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the condition in § 27920(b)(1) and § 27920(c)(1) that identifies who qualifies for each exemption; it does not restate every other numbered condition each subdivision separately imposes -- including the 30-day Department of Justice report and firearm safety certificate conditions in § 27920(b)(3)-(4) and § 27920(c)(3)-(4), and the age-18 condition in § 27920(b)(5) -- and it does not address the entirely separate import exemption in § 27920(d), which applies to firearms imported under 18 U.S.C. § 925(a)(4) and is unrelated to a decedent's estate. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own import exemption -- not a claim about federal firearms-import law generally, and not a claim about another state's law governing the same firearm before it reached California.

WHAT THIS INFORMATION SHEET DOES NOT DO
This information sheet states facts about a specific statutory exemption and the reporting conditions attached to it. It does not submit any report to the Department of Justice on behalf of Jordan Rivera, Casey Rivera, Alex Rivera, or anyone else, and completing it does not satisfy the 30-day reporting condition described elsewhere in this document. It does not determine whether Smith & Wesson Model 10 revolver, .38 Special, serial number ABC1234 in fact falls within a category the exemption covers, whether a specific person is a person prohibited by state or federal law from possessing a firearm, or whether a firearm addressed here is instead subject to separate federal regulation -- for example, under the National Firearms Act -- that this sheet does not address.
